description: How sediment grain size, shape and sorting record transport distance and depositional energy.
content_html:
Breaking Rocks Down: Weathering

Before sediment can travel anywhere, rock must first be broken apart. Weathering is the in-place breakdown of rock. It happens at or near the Earth’s surface where rock is exposed to the atmosphere, water and living organisms. Once weathered material is loosened from the parent rock, erosion picks it up and transport carries it away. Understanding these three linked stages — weathering, erosion, transport — is essential for interpreting the sedimentary rock record.

Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments without changing its chemistry. Freeze-thaw action is the most important process in cold climates: water in a crack expands by about 9% when it freezes, exerting pressure on the crack walls until the rock fragments. Repeated freeze-thaw produces angular boulders and scree slopes directly below cliffs.

Chemical weathering involves reactions between minerals and water, oxygen or acids. Feldspar is particularly susceptible to hydrolysis — it reacts with weakly acidic rainwater to produce clay minerals and dissolved ions. Calcite dissolves readily in acidic water (carbonation), which is why limestone landscapes develop karst features such as caves and sinkholes. Iron-bearing minerals oxidise to produce the red-brown iron oxides (haematite, goethite) that colour many red sedimentary sequences.

Grain Size: The Archive of Transport Energy

Grain size is the most directly readable record of the energy conditions in the transport system. High-energy environments — fast rivers, storm beaches, strong winds — move large particles; low-energy environments — deep water, slow rivers, quiet lagoons — deposit only fine particles. Grain size classifications run from boulders and gravel (coarsest) through sand to silt and clay (finest). These categories correspond to specific environments and are used to reconstruct depositional settings from ancient rocks.

Key Fact

Coarse grain size = high-energy transport (fast river, beach, wind). Fine grain size (silt/clay) = low-energy, quiet conditions (deep sea, lake, lagoon). Grain size directly records the energy of the depositional environment and is a primary tool for palaeo-environment reconstruction.

Grain Shape: Recording Transport Distance

Fresh sediment produced by weathering is angular — the sharp corners and edges that broke from the parent rock are still intact. As grains travel, they collide with each other and with the channel bed, gradually knocking off corners and edges. The result is progressive rounding. Rounding therefore indicates transport distance: angular grains have not travelled far; well-rounded grains have been transported over long distances or have been recycled through multiple sedimentary cycles.

The environment also matters: wind transport is much more effective at rounding grains than water transport because air provides less cushioning between grains. Wind-blown (aeolian) sand grains are typically frosted and well-rounded even over shorter distances; river sand grains take longer to round because they are partly cushioned by water. Scree deposits directly below a cliff contain angular fragments — they have barely moved.

Sorting: Reading Energy Consistency

Sorting describes how uniform grain sizes are within a deposit. Well-sorted sediment has a narrow range of grain sizes; poorly sorted sediment mixes coarse and fine together. Sorting reflects the consistency of the energy in the transport system. A beach exposed to regular wave action is highly sorted because the waves repeatedly winnow out fine grains, leaving only grains of similar size. A glacial till is extremely poorly sorted because ice carries everything from clay to boulders with equal indifference and dumps it all together when the ice melts.

Key Fact

Well-sorted = consistent energy environment (e.g. aeolian dune, wave-worked beach). Poorly sorted = variable or powerful depositional event (e.g. glacial till, debris flow). Sorting is a powerful clue to environment in sedimentary rock identification questions.

Screes: Angular, poorly sorted coarse fragments. Short transport, formed directly below cliffs by freeze-thaw. No rounding has occurred.

Rivers: Mixed grain sizes in active channels; gravel and sand bars in braided rivers; finer sands and silts on floodplains. Downstream, grain size decreases and rounding increases as transport distance grows.

Shallow seas: Sand-sized grains, well-sorted by wave and tidal action. Often shows ripple marks and cross-bedding.

Deep seas: Very fine silt and clay that has settled through the water column out of suspension. Also receives turbidite deposits — graded beds of sand to mud triggered by underwater avalanches.

Wind (aeolian) dunes: Well-sorted, fine to medium sand. Frosted, well-rounded grains; large-scale cross-bedding with a characteristic dune geometry.

Porosity is the proportion of empty space in a rock. Permeability is how well fluid can move through those spaces. These two properties are easily confused in exams but they measure different things. A rock can be porous without being permeable if the pores are not connected (for example, pumice has many pores but they are isolated bubbles). Conversely, a fractured rock may be permeable despite having low porosity if the fractures form a connected network.

Well-sorted coarse sandstone tends to have both high porosity (large connected pores) and high permeability (fluid passes easily). Clay-rich shale has very small, poorly connected pores — high porosity can exist but permeability is very low because the tiny pore spaces impede fluid flow. This distinction is critical when students answer questions about groundwater aquifers or reservoir rocks for oil and gas — mixing the two terms is a documented examiner concern.

The sediment properties covered in this lesson — grain size, shape and sorting, plus porosity and permeability — directly determine which sedimentary rock types form and what environments they record. The next lesson uses this foundation to classify the spec sedimentary rocks and to show how sedimentary structures like cross-bedding and graded bedding add further detail to palaeo-environment reconstruction.
exam_tip_html: Examiner reports flag the confusion between porosity and permeability as one of the highest-frequency errors in this unit. Always define them separately: porosity = percentage of pore space; permeability = ability of fluid to flow through. Then apply them correctly: a rock can be porous but not permeable (e.g. pumice). In questions about grain size and environment, remember to link grain size to energy: state the energy level, then give the grain size it produces. For sorting questions, give an environment example: well-sorted = beach or dune; poorly sorted = glacial deposit. Never say a rock is “permeable” as evidence it would make a good aquifer — also state that the pores must be connected.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Grain size records transport energy: coarse grains = high energy; fine grains = low energy. Grain shape records transport distance: angular = short distance; rounded = long distance. Sorting records energy consistency: well-sorted = uniform energy; poorly sorted = variable or powerful events.
  • Porosity (percentage pore space) and permeability (ability of fluid to pass through) are different properties. A rock can be porous but not permeable if pore spaces are not connected.
  • Different environments leave characteristic sediment signatures: screes (angular, poorly sorted), beaches (well-sorted sand), deep sea (fine clay/silt + turbidites), aeolian dunes (well-sorted, frosted, rounded sand).

practice_questions.text:
Which property describes the degree to which sediment grains are similar in size?
A) Rounding
B) Porosity
C) Sorting
D) Hardness
Name the process by which rock is broken down in situ at or near the Earth's surface without significant movement.
Describe what the grain shape of a sediment deposit tells a geologist about the history of the sediment.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- Angular grains indicate short transport distance / the sediment has not travelled far from the source
- Rounded / well-rounded grains indicate long transport distance / the grains have been abraded over a long distance or recycled through multiple sedimentary cycles
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between porosity and permeability and give one example of how they differ in a named rock type.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for:
- Porosity is the percentage of pore space in a rock (1 mark)
- Permeability is the ability of fluid to pass through the rock, requiring connected pore spaces (1 mark)
- Example: pumice has high porosity (many pores) but low permeability (pores are isolated bubbles); OR clay/shale has variable porosity but very low permeability because tiny pore spaces impede fluid flow (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the grain size, shape and sorting of sediment deposited in a wind-blown dune environment with sediment deposited as a scree at the base of a cliff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three properties compared contrastively for both environments: grain size (dune = fine to medium sand; scree = coarse, angular fragments varying in size); grain shape (dune = well-rounded, frosted; scree = angular, sharp edges); sorting (dune = well-sorted by wind winnowing; scree = poorly sorted, wide range of sizes). Stated as comparisons.
Secure: Two properties compared correctly for both environments.
Developing: One property compared correctly; or both environments described separately.
Emerging: One environment described with a grain property; other not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of grain size, shape and sorting as evidence for reconstructing the environment in which an ancient sedimentary rock was deposited.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three distinct lines of evidence evaluated with specific examples: (1) grain size indicates energy level (coarse = high energy rivers or beaches; fine = quiet deep water or lakes); (2) grain shape indicates transport distance and medium (rounded frosted = aeolian; rounded non-frosted = water; angular = scree/glacial); (3) sorting indicates energy consistency (well-sorted = beach or dune; poorly sorted = glacial or debris flow). Evaluative points about limitations (e.g. diagenesis/cementation can modify original porosity; multiple environments can produce similar grain sizes so one property alone is insufficient; well-rounded grains may be recycled not primary; colour from later oxidation may confuse interpretation).
Secure: Two lines of evidence with specific environments; some evaluation.
Developing: One line of evidence with partial environment link; limited evaluation.
Emerging: General statements about grain size with no specific environments or critical evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which property of sediment indicates the consistency of energy in the depositional environment?
What does well-rounded grain shape indicate about the history of a sediment?
options: Short transport distance from the source
Long transport distance with significant abrasion

knowledge_checks.q: The percentage of empty space between grains in a rock is called its _____.
Sediment deposited at the base of a cliff directly below the source is angular and poorly sorted, forming a feature called _____.
Match each depositional environment to its typical sediment properties:
right: Poorly sorted, angular, clay to boulder

flashcard_questions.q: What does angular grain shape tell you about a sediment's transport history?
flashcard_questions.a: Short transport distance; grains have not been significantly abraded

flashcard_questions.q: What does well-rounded grain shape tell you about a sediment's transport history?
flashcard_questions.a: Long transport distance or recycled through multiple sedimentary cycles

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between porosity and permeability?
flashcard_questions.a: Porosity = % pore space; permeability = ability of fluid to flow through connected pores

flashcard_questions.q: What grain properties are typical of wind-blown (aeolian) sand dunes?
What grain properties are typical of glacial till?
flashcard_questions.a: Poorly sorted, angular grains ranging from clay to boulders

flashcard_questions.q: Why does coarse grain size indicate a high-energy depositional environment?
flashcard_questions.a: Only high-energy transport (fast rivers, strong waves) can carry large, heavy grains
In-place breakdown of rock by physical, chemical or biological processes without significant movement

flashcard_questions.q: Why is sorting a useful indicator of depositional environment?
flashcard_questions.a: Well-sorted = consistent energy (beach, dune); poorly sorted = variable or powerful events (glacial, debris flow)

flashcard_questions.q: Can a rock be porous but not permeable? Give an example.
flashcard_questions.a: Yes — pumice has many pores but they are isolated, so fluid cannot flow through

glossary_terms.definition: The breakdown of rock in situ by physical, chemical or biological processes, without significant movement of the material.
A measure of the average particle size in a sediment or sedimentary rock, ranging from boulder through gravel, sand, silt to clay.
The degree to which the corners and edges of a sediment grain have been smoothed by abrasion during transport.
The degree to which sediment grains are similar in size; well-sorted sediment has a narrow range of grain sizes, poorly sorted sediment has a wide range.
The percentage of a rock's total volume that consists of pore spaces between grains or in fractures.
The ability of a rock to allow fluid to pass through it, dependent on whether pore spaces are connected.
